evals.prompt: Define design module composition in 2-3 sentences. Name the four mainstream patterns it covers.
expected_elements: Defines it as shaping a reusable component's API so variation comes from composing parts, not configuration props
Names compound components (parent + named children sharing context)
Names slot/children APIs and render props / function-as-children
Names headless primitives (state and behavior exposed, markup/styling delegated)

evals.prompt: Why is the shared context contract — not the prop signatures — described as the real API of a compound-component module?
expected_elements: Compound pieces share state through context (React context or framework equivalent)
The context contract is what the parent provides and the children expect
Changing the contract is a breaking change even when prop signatures stay the same
Children require the parent's context — they cannot render correctly outside it

evals.prompt: What is the trade-off between a configuration (prop-heavy) API and a composition API, and how do mature systems often resolve it?
expected_elements: Prop-heavy API is fast for the common case but friction-heavy for unanticipated variants
Composition API costs more typing for the common case but absorbs variants with no friction
Every boolean prop is a decision the author imposes on every consumer; a slot defers the decision
Mature systems often offer both: a high-level summary component built on low-level composable primitives

evals.prompt: A Card component has 14 boolean props and keeps growing as new variants are requested. How should an agent redesign its API?
expected_elements: Move to a composition API (e.g. Card with Card.Header / Card.Body / Card.Footer or slots)
Reduce boolean props to single digits; let consumers compose unanticipated variants
Distinguish variants that are part of the module's identity (prop) from how a consumer uses it (slot)
Optionally keep a high-level convenience component over the composable primitives

evals.prompt: Explain the asChild / polymorphic pattern: what it does, what problem it solves, and what care it requires.
expected_elements: Lets a consumer change the rendered element while inheriting all behavior and ARIA wiring
Collapses two-level wrappers and avoids the 'button inside button' accessibility error
Requires the parent to clone or render-prop its single child carefully
Behavior and ARIA attributes must be preserved across the element swap

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the design-module-composition skill to decide which folder the OrderDetailPage lives in and which app owns it. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — that is application-level architecture (frontend-architecture)
This skill owns the composition API shape of a reusable module, not file/feature placement
Correctly distinguishes how a module exposes its parts from where modules live and which app owns a screen
Redirects to frontend-architecture

evals.prompt: A developer says 'composition just means adding more props so the component can do more.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: Adding props is configuration, not composition — every prop is a decision imposed on every consumer
Composition exposes parts (slots, compound children, headless state) so consumers assemble unanticipated variants
Adding props makes the common case faster but every unforeseen variant a fork
Composition is about deferring decisions, not multiplying the configuration surface

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a component module is well-composed?
expected_elements: Primary variations are achievable by composing children, not boolean props; boolean-prop count is single digits
Compound children render outside the parent only with an explicit error (they need the parent's context)
Accessibility wiring (aria-controls, aria-expanded, focus return) is the module's responsibility, even under asChild/headless
asChild/polymorphic element swaps preserve all behavior and ARIA; the module composes into a non-obvious shape without modification
